# Part I: Track-Level Features 

## Class Corpus Chart I Tempo-Arousal

### Class Corpus Chart I Tempo-Arousal



```{r}

specific_songs <- compmus2025 |> filter(filename %in% c("onni-q-1", "onni-q-2"))
other_songs <- compmus2025 |> filter(!filename %in% c("onni-q-1", "onni-q-2"))

p <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = other_songs,
    aes(
      x = tempo,
      y = arousal,
      size = arousal,
      colour = arousal,
      text = filename
    )
  ) +
  geom_point( # Add a separate layer for the specific songs
    data = specific_songs,
    aes(
      x = tempo,
      y = arousal,
      colour = arousal,
      text = filename
    ),
    shape = 16, # Use a different shape (e.g., triangle)
    stroke = 1.5, # Add a border
    colour = "red" # Use a distinct color
  ) +
  geom_rug(data = other_songs, linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(50, 150),
    breaks = c(50, 75, 100, 125, 150),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(3, 8),
    breaks = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 8),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  scale_size_continuous(
    trans = "exp",
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light() +
  labs(
    x = "Tempo",
    y = "Arousal",
    colour = "Arousal"
  )

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")

```


  
### Findings:

<p>
With Chart I, I intend to illustrate the relation between the tempo of a song and its arousal.
</p>

<p>
Chart I indicates that the increase of tempo does not necessarily contribute to the increase of a song's arousal. Instead, it seems that most songs that sound more exciting and stimulating than others tend to have a tempo close to 100bpm.
</p>

<p>This means that there is a strong relation between valence and arousal.</p>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Class Corpus Chart II Tempo-Valence

### Class Corpus Chart II Tempo-Valence

```{r}

specific_songs <- compmus2025 |> filter(filename %in% c("onni-q-1", "onni-q-2"))
other_songs <- compmus2025 |> filter(!filename %in% c("onni-q-1", "onni-q-2"))

p <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = other_songs,
    aes(
      x = tempo,
      y = valence,
      size = valence,
      colour = valence,
      text = filename
    )
  ) +
  geom_point( # Add a separate layer for the specific songs
    data = specific_songs,
    aes(
      x = tempo,
      y = valence,
      colour = valence,
      text = filename
    ),
    shape = 16, # Use a different shape (e.g., triangle)
    stroke = 1.5, # Add a border
    colour = "red" # Use a distinct color
  ) +
  geom_rug(data = other_songs, linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(50, 150),
    breaks = c(50, 75, 100, 125, 150),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(3, 8),
    breaks = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 8),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  scale_size_continuous(
    trans = "exp",
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light() +
  labs(
    x = "Tempo",
    y = "Valence",
    colour = "Valence"
  )

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")

```


### Findings:

<p>
With Chart II, I intend to illustrate the relation between the valence of a song and its arousal.
</p>

<p>
Chart II indicates that the increase of valence does clearly contribute to the increase of a song's arousal. Indeed, it seems that the more positive and pleasant a piece of music sound, the more exciting and stimulating it would be.
</p>

### Findings:

<p>With Chart III, I intend to illustrate the relations between these factors: approachability, arousal, valence, and engagingness. According to Chart III, it is clear that with the increase in approachability, there does not occurs a similar change in arousal, valence, as well as engagingness, vice versa.</p>

<p>
Chart III indicates a weak relation between approachability and the other three features. More importantly, this means that whether or not a piece of music is exciting has very little to do with its approachability.
</p>
